hints: Think about what happens to the C=C double bond when $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ from water add across it, is anything lost or is everything joined together.
walkthrough:
See what joins together**
Picture propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$, and water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. In this reaction the $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ both end up attached to the carbon skeleton to give $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$. Nothing else is formed, two molecules simply combine into one.

hints: Recall which strong acid provides $\text{H}^+$ for the industrial hydration of alkenes to alcohols.
Think about what form the water must be in and what temperature is needed for a gaseous alkene to react.
walkthrough:
Supply the source of $\text{H}^+$**
Alkenes need an acid to start electrophilic addition with water. In the lab and industry you use concentrated sulfuric acid, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, or phosphoric(V) acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, which provides the $\text{H}^+$ catalyst.

Get water to react as steam**
Water is used as steam, not cold liquid water, with heating. High temperature gives the particles enough energy to react, and pressure is often applied to keep the gaseous mixture together.

Final answer: catalyst: concentrated sulfuric acid or phosphoric(V) acid
conditions: steam with heat (high pressure also used)

hints: Remember that every single bond is one $\sigma$ bond, while every double bond is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$ bond.
Draw out $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and count every $\text{C-H}$, $\text{C-C}$, $\text{C-O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ link.
walkthrough:
Count propene, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$**
Draw $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. Count single links first. There are 6 $\text{C-H}$ bonds, each is $1\sigma$. There is 1 $\text{C-C}$ single bond, $1\sigma$. The $\text{C=C}$ double bond is $1\sigma + 1\pi$. Add the $\sigma$ bonds: $6 + 1 + 1 = 8$. So $\sigma = 8$, $\pi = 1$.

Count the alcohol, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$**
The product is a saturated alcohol with only single bonds, for example propanol. Count: 2 $\text{C-C}$ bonds ($2\sigma$), 7 $\text{C-H}$ bonds ($7\sigma$), 1 $\text{C-O}$ bond ($1\sigma$), 1 $\text{O-H}$ bond ($1\sigma$). Total $\sigma = 2 + 7 + 1 + 1 = 11$. With no double bond, $\pi = 0$.

hints: Imagine $\text{H}^+$ adding to the $\text{C=C}$ in propene in two ways, putting the $\text{H}$ on the end carbon in one case and on the middle carbon in the other.
Identify which carbocation has the $\text{C}^+$ joined to two other carbons and which has it joined to only one other carbon.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward a positive centre to stabilise it.
walkthrough:
Draw the two possible $\text{H}^+$ additions**
Start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the end $\text{CH}_2$ carbon, you get $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+(\text{H})\text{CH}_3$. The positive carbon is attached to two other carbons, a secondary carbocation. If $\text{H}^+$ adds to the middle $\text{CH}$ carbon, you get $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+(\text{H}_2)$. The positive carbon is attached to only one other carbon, a primary carbocation.

Feel why positive charge needs help**
A carbocation has a carbon with only six electrons and a full positive charge. It is electron hungry. Anything that can push electron density toward it will spread out that charge and lower its energy, making it more stable.

Compare alkyl donation**
Alkyl groups like $\text{CH}_3$ have a positive inductive effect, they push electrons toward the $\text{C}^+$. The secondary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+(\text{H})\text{CH}_3$ has two alkyl groups donating, while the primary ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+(\text{H}_2)$ has only one. Greater electron donation means greater stabilisation, so the secondary carbocation is more stable.

Final answer: more stable: $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+(\text{H})\text{CH}_3$ (secondary carbocation)
less stable: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}^+(\text{H}_2)$ (primary carbocation)
The secondary ion is stabilised by the greater positive inductive effect / electron donation from two alkyl groups compared to one.

hints: Remember water attacks the more stable carbocation, so the $\text{OH}$ ends up on the carbon that carried the positive charge.
walkthrough:
Follow the more stable route**
In step 2, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ attacks the more stable secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{C}^+(\text{H})\text{CH}_3$. The $\text{OH}$ therefore finishes on the middle carbon, giving $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, which is propan-2-ol.

hints: Look at 2-bromopropane losing $\text{HBr}$ to form the $\text{C=C}$ in propene, a small molecule is removed from one molecule.
walkthrough:
Spot the reverse of addition**
Here $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$ loses $\text{H}$ and $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$. A small molecule is removed and a double bond is created. That is the hallmark of elimination.

hints: Recall which base is used to remove $\text{HBr}$ from a halogenoalkane, $\text{NaOH}$ or $\text{KOH}$.
Think about how to favour elimination over substitution by changing the solvent from water to alcohol and using heat.
walkthrough:
Choose the strong base**
You need hydroxide to pull off $\text{H}^+$ while $\text{Br}^-$ leaves. Use sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH}$, or potassium hydroxide, $\text{KOH}$.

Create eliminating conditions**
Dissolve that base in ethanol, not water, to make ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$, and heat the mixture. Aqueous conditions and low temperature favour substitution to an alcohol, while ethanolic solution plus heat favours elimination to the alkene.

Final answer: reagents: $\text{NaOH}$ / $\text{KOH}$
conditions: in ethanolic / alcoholic solution with heat
